howToEdit: Each question: q = question, a = right answer, w = two wrong answers, means/example/why/trick = teaching text, whyNot = one line per wrong answer (same order as w), src = where the fact comes from, mem = true if it's pure memorization, verify = note if Nika should confirm. Keep answers under about 22 characters so they fit on the road.

verifyWithNika.note: Niko's example asked 'LPU65 can be sold until what age?' The materials don't give LPU65 issue ages. Get the real range from Nika or the rate sheet, then add the question.
Training page says coverage lasts until 18. The 2.1 review quiz said 21. Not quizzed until Nika confirms.
A handout shows hospital $1,200/day, ICU $2,400/day, ER $600, AD&D $120k adult / $24k child. Official training says $100-$500 levels. Game uses the official training numbers.
Training says $400/month for 6 months. Does it scale with the A71000 level?
Max issue age for seniors (80.5 heard, not confirmed).
Training 2.1 says 10% to 85%. Training 1.2 says up to 80%. Not quizzed.
Efe said grandparents can only add $25k. Training only says over $25k total needs the Child Coverage Questionnaire.
Week 1 material. Add questions once Niko has the real WL/PR/EX/SL thresholds.
Waiver of premium cost (~$3-4?), layoff vs strike waivers, who qualifies.

verifyWithNika.topic: A71 on every policy / ALP to AP
verifyWithNika.note: Late Dec 2026 change. How AP counts the A71000.
Mentor notes: $15k starter, $25-30k with inflation. Not quizzed until confirmed.

questions.q: Client on the $300 A71000 level sprains an ankle and goes to the ER. What does the plan pay?
questions.means: The A71000 pays ER and outpatient care at half the plan level, per injury.
questions.example: Think of a gym day pass at half price: same gym, half the number. $300 level, half is $150.
questions.why: Half of $300 is $150, paid in cash to the client for that injury.
whyNot: $300 is the full level. That's what one hospital day pays, not an ER visit.
$600 is double the level. That's an ICU day in the first 14 days.

questions.q: Client on the $400 level is admitted to the hospital (not ICU) for 3 days after a car accident. Total paid?
questions.means: A hospital stay pays the full plan level for every day, up to 365 days.
questions.example: Like rent by the night: $400 a night, 3 nights, $1,200.
questions.why: $400 times 3 days is $1,200.
whyNot: $600 uses the ER rule (half the level) times 3. Hospital days pay the full level.
$2,400 doubles it. Double only applies to ICU days, and only the first 14.
questions.trick: Hospital = Hotel rate: full level per night.

questions.q: $500 level. After a bad fall the client spends 20 days in the ICU. Total ICU benefit?
questions.means: ICU pays double the level per day for the first 14 days, then the full level per day after that.
questions.example: Like a phone plan with 14 days of double data, then normal data.
questions.why: 14 days at $1,000 is $14,000. 6 more days at $500 is $3,000. Total $17,000.
whyNot: $20,000 pays double for all 20 days. The double rate stops after day 14.
$10,000 pays the normal level all 20 days and forgets the double first 14.
questions.trick: ICU: 14 doubled, then back to normal.

questions.q: How many ICU days does the A71000 pay at DOUBLE the plan level?
questions.means: The double ICU rate covers the first 14 days of an ICU stay.
questions.example: Two weeks of double pay, like overtime that only lasts two weeks.
questions.why: Training: double the level per day for the first 14 days, then the full level.
whyNot: 10 days is the wrong answer on the official 2.2 review quiz. It's 14.
30 days is a month. The double window is two weeks.

questions.q: After the 14 doubled ICU days, the A71000 keeps paying the full level for up to how many MORE days?
questions.means: After day 14 the ICU benefit drops to the full level for up to another 351 days.
questions.example: 14 plus 351 is 365, one full year, like a yearly gym membership.
questions.why: 14 + 351 = 365. The total ICU window is one year.
whyNot: 365 is the total year. After 14 days are used, 351 are left.
186 is half a year plus change. Not a number in the plan.
questions.trick: 14 + 351 = 365. The year is the whole ride.

questions.q: What's the most hospital days (non-ICU) the A71000 pays for one stay?
questions.means: Hospital stays pay the full plan level per day for up to 365 days.
questions.example: A full year of daily pay, like a 365-day streak in a game.
questions.why: Training: full plan level per day, up to 365 days.
whyNot: 180 days is half a year. The plan pays up to a full year.
90 days is a common limit at other carriers, not the A71000.

questions.q: B2000 on a $300 A71000. The client dies in a car crash. What does the B2000 pay?
questions.means: The B2000 is the accidental death benefit built into every A71000. Base = level x 100. Auto = 2x base. Common carrier = 5x base.
questions.example: $300 plus two zeros is $30,000. Car crash doubles it to $60,000.
questions.why: $300 x 100 = $30,000 base. Auto-related doubles it: $60,000.
whyNot: $30,000 is the base. That's for a non-auto accident, like falling off a ladder.
$150,000 is 5x the base. That's a common carrier death, like a bus, train or plane.
questions.trick: Add two zeros, then: Car = 2, Carrier = 5.

questions.q: B2000 on a $200 A71000. The client dies as a passenger in a commercial bus crash. Payout?
questions.means: A commercial bus, train or plane is a common carrier. The B2000 pays 5x the base for it.
questions.example: $200 plus two zeros is $20,000. Bus = common carrier = x5 = $100,000.
whyNot: $40,000 is the auto rate (2x). A commercial bus is a common carrier, which pays 5x.
$20,000 is the base, for a non-auto accident.

questions.q: B2000 on a $500 A71000. The client falls off a ladder at home and dies. Payout?
questions.means: A non-auto, non-common-carrier accident pays the B2000 base: plan level x 100.
questions.example: $500 plus two zeros is $50,000.
questions.why: A ladder fall is a regular accidental death, so it pays the base: $50,000.
whyNot: $100,000 is the auto-related amount (2x).
$250,000 is the common carrier amount (5x).
questions.trick: No car, no carrier: just add two zeros.

questions.q: Hospital Recoupment Rider: the most it pays after one hospital stay?
questions.means: The Recoupment Rider pays $400 a month after a hospital stay, for up to 6 months, to help during recovery.
questions.example: Like a $400 car payment covered for 6 months while you heal.
whyNot: $1,200 is only 3 months.
$4,800 is 12 months. The rider stops at 6.
questions.verify: Training gives $400/month. Ask Nika if that amount changes with the plan level.

questions.q: Client gets a bad respiratory infection and goes to urgent care. What does the A71000 pay?
questions.means: The A71000 is accident-only. Sickness isn't covered at all.
questions.example: Car insurance pays for a crash, not for your engine wearing out. A71000 pays for getting hurt, not getting sick.
questions.why: No accident, no benefit. An infection is an illness.
whyNot: Half the level is the ER rule, but only for an accidental injury.
The A71000 never reimburses bills. It pays set cash amounts, and only for accidents.
questions.trick: Get HURT, get paid. Get sick, no.

questions.q: A mom wants the A71000 for herself, her husband and their 2 kids. What's true?
questions.means: The A71000 comes as an individual plan or a family plan.
questions.example: Like a family phone plan: one plan, everybody on it.
questions.why: Training: available as either an individual or family plan.
whyNot: False. That's the trick statement on the official 2.2 review quiz.
Kids can be on the family plan.

questions.q: When the A71000 pays out, who gets the money?
questions.means: It's an indemnity plan: a set amount per event, paid to the client to spend however they want.
questions.example: Like a gift card that works anywhere: rent, groceries, the electric bill.
questions.why: Training: pays the client directly, not a reimbursement of bills.
whyNot: The hospital is paid by health insurance. A71000 money goes to the client.
A reimbursement pays back exact bills. A71000 pays set amounts no matter the bill.

questions.q: How many A71000 levels are there?
questions.means: There are five levels: $100, $200, $300, $400, $500. Every benefit scales with the level.
questions.example: Like five sizes of the same pizza. Bigger size, bigger slices everywhere.
questions.why: Training lists exactly five levels, $100 through $500.
whyNot: Three is too few. The levels go all the way to $500.
There's no $50 level and no 10 levels.

questions.q: Dad has $200,000 of life coverage, Mom has $60,000. Max Head Start on their child?
questions.means: Head Start max = the smaller of (half the higher parent) and (the lower parent's total). Never below $25,000.
questions.example: Two speed limits on one road: you follow the lower one.
questions.why: Half of Dad's $200k is $100k. Mom's total is $60k. The smaller is $60,000.
whyNot: $100,000 is half of Dad's, but Mom's $60k is lower, so it caps the child.
$25,000 is the floor. It only kicks in when the math lands under $25k.
questions.trick: Half the high, all the low, take the low.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: Dad has $80,000. Mom has no life insurance. Max Head Start on their child?
questions.means: Every child can get up to $25,000 of Head Start even if a parent has no coverage. That's the floor.
questions.example: Like a minimum wage: the math can say less, but nobody goes under the floor.
questions.why: Half of Dad's is $40k, Mom's is $0, smaller is $0, so the $25,000 floor applies.
whyNot: $40,000 is half of Dad's, but Mom's $0 is lower.
$0 is the raw math, but the $25,000 floor beats it.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: Mom has $150,000, Dad has $120,000. Max Head Start on their child?
questions.means: Take half of the HIGHER parent and compare it to the LOWER parent's full amount.
questions.example: Mom's the bigger plan here. Half of her $150k is $75k.
questions.why: Half of Mom's $150k is $75k. Dad's total is $120k. The smaller is $75,000.
whyNot: $120,000 is Dad's full amount, but half of Mom's is smaller.
$60,000 is half of the LOWER parent. You halve the higher one, not the lower one.
questions.trick: Halve the high one, never the low one.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: A child's Head Start max works out to $40,000. The child already has $10,000 of active whole life. How much more can you add?
questions.means: The Head Start max includes any whole life already active on that child.
questions.example: A $40 gift card limit with $10 already spent: you have $30 left.
questions.why: $40,000 max minus the $10,000 already in force = $30,000.
whyNot: $40,000 ignores the $10k already on the child. Existing whole life counts.
$50,000 adds them together. The max is a ceiling, not a starting point.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: Parents put $15,000 of Head Start on their son. Grandma wants to add $15,000 more. What does that trigger?
questions.means: Going over $25,000 of total Head Start on one child needs a Child Coverage Questionnaire. It counts everyone's purchases together.
questions.example: Like a weekly data cap shared by the whole family: it's the total that counts.
questions.why: $15k + $15k = $30k total, which is over $25k, so the questionnaire is required.
whyNot: Each purchase is under $25k, but the rule is cumulative across parents and grandparents.
Training names the questionnaire, not an exam.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: How much coverage does the child rider give each child?
questions.means: The child rider adds $10,000 of term coverage on each eligible child, on the parent's policy.
questions.example: Ten grand per kid, like each kid getting the same size slice.
questions.why: Training: $10,000 of coverage on each eligible child.
whyNot: $5,000 is too low for the AIL child rider.
$25,000 is the Head Start floor, a different product.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: Family has 4 kids. How many child rider premiums do they pay?
questions.means: One child rider covers every eligible child in the household for one premium.
questions.example: Like a family Netflix plan: one price, the whole house watches.
questions.why: Training: one rider covers all eligible children for one premium, no matter how many.
whyNot: Per-child pricing is Head Start, where each child gets their own policy.
There's no two-premium cap. It's one premium, period.
questions.trick: One rider, one price, all the kids.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: The child rider lets a child convert to permanent coverage with no medical questions, up to how much?
questions.means: The child can convert up to five times the rider amount without proving insurability.
questions.why: Training: up to five times the rider amount, which is $50,000.
whyNot: $25,000 is the Head Start floor, not the conversion amount.
$100,000 would be 10 times. The rule is 5 times.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: How young can a child be covered by the child rider?
questions.means: Child rider coverage starts at 15 days old.
questions.example: About two weeks after the baby comes home from the hospital.
questions.why: Training: covers children from 15 days old.
whyNot: Not at birth. There's a 15-day wait.
6 months is too long. It's 15 days.
questions.trick: Fifteen days: two weeks and a day.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: Which kids' coverage builds cash value?
questions.means: Head Start is whole life on the child, so it builds cash value. The child rider is term: pure protection.
questions.example: Head Start is buying the car. The child rider is renting it.
questions.why: Training: the child rider has no cash value. Head Start is the child's own permanent policy.
whyNot: The child rider is term coverage with no cash value.
Only Head Start builds cash value.
questions.trick: Head Start = whole life = cash. Rider = rental.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: Mom's policy with the child rider lapses. What happens to the kids' rider coverage?
questions.means: The child rider is tied to the parent's policy. If the parent's policy lapses or is cancelled, the rider ends.
questions.example: Like a phone case: lose the phone, the case doesn't make calls.
questions.why: Training: ends if the parent's policy lapses or is cancelled.
whyNot: It can't survive on its own. It's attached to the parent's policy.
Conversion is an option the family uses, not something automatic.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: Children placed into Head Start whole life must be under what age?
questions.means: Children under 18 are enrolled in whole life through the Head Start program.
questions.example: Same line as being a legal adult.
questions.why: Training: when enrolling children under 18, they go into Head Start.
whyNot: 21 is the number that shows up in the child rider confusion. Head Start is under 18.
16 is driving age, not the Head Start cutoff.
questions.trick: Head Start ends where adulthood starts: 18.

questions.q: Which one is NOT an AIL whole life rate bracket?
questions.means: AIL's whole life brackets are Regular (WL), Preferred (PR), Executive (EX) and Select Life (SL).
questions.example: Like coffee sizes with their own names. 'Standard' isn't on this menu.
questions.why: Standard (ST) isn't one of the four. The four are WL, PR, EX, SL.
whyNot: Preferred (PR) is a real bracket.
Executive (EX) is a real bracket.
questions.trick: We Pray Every Sunday: WL, PR, EX, SL.

questions.q: Client steps up to a bigger whole life amount. What happens to the cost per dollar of coverage?
questions.means: More coverage moves the client into a better rate bracket, so each dollar of coverage costs less.
questions.example: Like a Costco pack: the bigger pack costs more total but less per item.
questions.why: Training: the more coverage, the better the rate per dollar.
whyNot: Most clients expect that, but brackets make bigger amounts cheaper per dollar.
That's the opposite of how AIL brackets work.
questions.trick: Bigger pack, better price per piece.

questions.q: What's the total whole life coverage cap for senior clients?
questions.means: Senior clients have a total coverage cap of $35,000.
questions.example: Like a $35k ceiling. You can't stack past it.
questions.why: Training lists the senior cap as $35,000 total.
whyNot: $50,000 is the child rider conversion amount.
$25,000 is the Head Start floor.

questions.q: Graded Benefit Whole Life, $20,000 face. The client dies in year 2. What does it pay?
questions.means: Graded benefit pays 25% of the face in year 1, 50% in year 2, 75% in year 3, and 100% after that.
questions.example: Like a new phone that unlocks features over time.
whyNot: $5,000 is 25%, the year 1 amount.
$20,000 is the full face. That's only after year 3.
questions.trick: 25, 50, 75, 100. Count up a quarter a year.

questions.q: Graded Benefit Whole Life, $15,000 face. Death in year 3. Payout?
questions.means: Year 3 of a graded benefit policy pays 75% of the face.
questions.example: Three quarters of a pizza is 75%.
whyNot: $7,500 is 50%, the year 2 amount.
$15,000 is 100%, which starts after year 3.

questions.q: What does a senior get in exchange for the graded payout schedule?
questions.means: Graded benefit has more lenient underwriting. In exchange, the full death benefit phases in over the first years.
questions.example: Like a car loan with easy approval but a waiting period on some perks.
questions.why: Training: more lenient underwriting is the defining feature; the graded schedule is the trade-off.
whyNot: The training never says it's cheaper. The trade is about qualifying.
Nothing in the training ties graded benefit to faster cash value.

questions.q: With LPU65, what stops at age 65?
questions.means: LPU65 is limited-pay whole life: you pay until 65, and you're covered for life.
questions.example: Like paying off a car loan: the payments end, you still own the car.
questions.why: Payments end at 65. Coverage keeps going for life.
whyNot: Coverage doesn't end. That's term to 65, a different product.
Cash value stays in the policy. It doesn't stop at 65.
questions.trick: 65 and done paying, never done covered.

questions.q: LPU65 vs regular whole life, same face amount, same client. Which costs more per month?
questions.means: LPU65 squeezes the payments into fewer years, so the monthly premium is higher. Cash value builds faster.
questions.example: Paying a car off in 3 years costs more a month than in 6, but you're done sooner.
questions.why: Fewer years of payments means a higher monthly payment.
whyNot: Regular whole life spreads payments over a lifetime, so the monthly is lower.
Same face, fewer payment years, so it can't be the same.
questions.trick: Pay faster, pay more a month.

questions.q: Which plan is final-expense whole life where the benefit can be assigned to a funeral home?
questions.means: Freedom of Choice is final-expense whole life with a funeral-home assignment option.
questions.example: Like prepaying your favorite restaurant so the bill's covered when the family shows up.
questions.why: Per Niko's notes, Freedom of Choice pairs whole life with a funeral-home assignment.
whyNot: Graded Benefit is the lenient-underwriting senior plan. It's about qualifying, not funeral assignment.
Head Start is whole life on a child.
questions.trick: Freedom of Choice: choose your funeral home.

questions.q: Which AIL term option has a coverage amount that shrinks over the years?
questions.means: Decreasing term lowers the coverage over time, like a mortgage balance going down.
questions.example: Like a car loan: the balance shrinks every year, so does the coverage.
questions.why: Training: decreasing term is used for mortgage protection because the debt also decreases.
whyNot: 20-year term keeps the same coverage for 20 years.
Term to 65 keeps coverage until 65.

questions.q: On AIL's 10-year term, what does 'renewable' mean?
questions.means: Renewable means the client can extend coverage at the end of the term without a new medical exam.
questions.example: Like renewing your lease without a new credit check.
questions.why: Training: renewable = extend coverage at the end of the term without a new medical exam.
whyNot: Switching to whole life is 'convertible', the other half of R&C.
Renewable doesn't promise the price stays the same.

questions.q: On AIL's term, what does 'convertible' mean?
questions.means: Convertible means the client can turn the term policy into permanent coverage like whole life, without new medical underwriting.
questions.example: Like turning a car lease into a purchase without a new credit check.
questions.why: Training: convert into a permanent policy without new medical underwriting.
whyNot: Extending the term is 'renewable'.
Converting to whole life usually costs more, not less.

questions.q: Which AIL term options does training call renewable AND convertible?
questions.means: Training names the 4-year and 10-year term options as renewable and convertible.
questions.example: The short leases come with the easy re-up.
questions.why: Training: for both the 4-year and 10-year term options, renewable and convertible is its own selling point.
whyNot: Training doesn't describe 20-year or term to 65 as R&C.
Decreasing term is the mortgage-style one.

questions.q: Client, 40, wants level coverage for exactly the 20 years left on her mortgage. Best fit?
questions.means: 20-year term gives level coverage for a 20-year window, commonly matched to a mortgage.
questions.example: Like a 20-year phone contract that matches the 20-year loan.
questions.why: She asked for LEVEL coverage for exactly 20 years. That's 20-year term.
whyNot: Decreasing term also fits mortgages, but the coverage shrinks. She wants level.
Term to 65 at age 40 runs 25 years, longer than she needs.
questions.trick: Match the term to the timeline.

questions.q: Client asks: 'Does term build cash value like whole life?'
questions.means: Term is temporary, pure protection. Whole life is permanent and builds cash value.
questions.example: Renting an apartment: you're protected while you pay, but you don't build equity.
questions.why: Training: term offers neither permanence nor cash value.
whyNot: There's no cash value at year 10. That's a made-up feature.
Renewing extends the term. It doesn't add cash value.

questions.q: At AIL, the ADB rider ends at what age?
questions.means: The ADB rider ends at 70 at AIL. The base policy keeps going.
questions.example: Like a phone warranty that ends while you keep the phone.
questions.why: Training: in our company that age is 70 years old.
whyNot: 65 is LPU65's payment age, not when ADB ends.
80 is too old. ADB stops at 70.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Deep Dive Accidental Death Benefits

questions.q: Which death would the ADB rider pay on?
questions.means: ADB pays only when the death comes directly from a covered accident.
questions.example: A crash you didn't cause is an accident. Illness and overdoses aren't covered.
questions.why: A car crash is a covered accident.
whyNot: Drug overdose is a listed exclusion.
A heart attack is illness, not an accident, even if it happens at the gym.
questions.trick: Accident only. No illness, no overdose.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Deep Dive Accidental Death Benefits

questions.q: Client has $50,000 whole life + $50,000 ADB. He dies of cancer. What's paid?
questions.means: ADB pays extra only for accidental death. A cancer death pays the base policy only.
questions.example: The base is your main meal; ADB is the dessert that only comes with an accident.
questions.why: Cancer is illness, so only the $50,000 base pays.
whyNot: $100,000 would be an accidental death (base + ADB).
The base whole life still pays. ADB just doesn't add anything.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Deep Dive Accidental Death Benefits

questions.q: For ADB to pay, the death usually has to happen within how long of the accident?
questions.means: The death usually has to happen within a set time after the accident, commonly 90 to 365 days.
questions.example: Like a return window on a purchase: it has to happen inside the window.
questions.why: Training: commonly 90 to 365 days, depending on the policy.
whyNot: 30 days is too short.
2 years is the contestability period, a different rule.
questions.trick: ADB window: one season to one year.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Deep Dive Accidental Death Benefits

questions.q: Does the ADB rider build cash value?
questions.means: ADB has no cash value. It's pure protection on top of the base.
questions.example: Like a phone insurance add-on: no money back if you never use it.
questions.why: Training: no cash value, it's pure protection.
whyNot: The base whole life builds cash value. The ADB rider doesn't.
At 70 the ADB rider ends. Nothing builds.
questions.trick: ADB = protection only, no piggy bank.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Deep Dive Accidental Death Benefits

questions.q: Terminal Illness Accelerated Death Benefit rider. What's the deal in New Jersey?
questions.means: The Terminal Illness rider pays 1/2 the face early when a doctor certifies 12 months or less to live, but it's not offered in NJ.
questions.example: Like a menu item the restaurant doesn't serve in this state.
questions.why: Training: this rider is not available in NJ.
whyNot: Half the face is how it works in states that have it. NJ doesn't.
It never pays the full face early, and NJ doesn't offer it anyway.

questions.q: Healthy 26-year-old worried he'll want more coverage later. Which rider protects that?
questions.means: Guaranteed Insurability Option lets him buy more coverage later at set points with no new medical underwriting.
questions.example: Like reserving a parking spot: it's yours later even if the lot fills up.
questions.why: GIO protects his future ability to add coverage, whatever happens to his health.
whyNot: Spousal covers a spouse, not his own future increases.
Child rider covers kids.
questions.trick: GIO = Get It Over-and-over, no exam.

questions.q: Client's plan should cover his wife without a separate policy on her. Which rider?
questions.means: The Spousal Rider extends coverage to the spouse under the primary policyholder's plan.
questions.example: Like adding your partner to your car insurance.
questions.why: Training: the Spousal Rider covers a spouse under the policyholder's plan.
whyNot: GIO protects his own future increases.
Head Start is whole life on a child.
questions.trick: Spouse = Spousal. Easy one, don't overthink.

questions.q: In states where the Terminal Illness rider exists, how long must a doctor say the insured has left?
questions.means: The TI rider triggers when a physician certifies 12 months or less to live (24 in IL, MA, WA). Not sold in NJ.
questions.example: One year on the calendar.
questions.why: Training: 12 months or less, 24 months in IL, MA and WA.
whyNot: 24 months is only in Illinois, Massachusetts and Washington.
6 months is hospice-style language, not this rider.
questions.trick: TI = one year (two in IL, MA, WA). Never NJ.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the C20 lump sum choices?
questions.means: The C20 pays one lump sum at $10,000, $20,000 or $50,000.
questions.example: Three sizes: small, medium, large. No $25k size.
questions.why: $25,000 isn't on the list. It's the wrong answer on the official 2.2 review quiz.
whyNot: $20,000 is a real C20 choice.
$50,000 is a real C20 choice.

questions.q: A client's C20 pays out. A year later the cancer comes back. What does the C20 do?
questions.means: The C20 pays one lump sum on a first-time diagnosis, then the plan ends.
questions.example: A one-time bonus check: once it's cashed, it's done.
questions.why: Training: once the C20 pays out, the plan ends. No recurrence payout.
whyNot: Paying again on recurrence is the C10's strength.
Treatment coverage (up to 500 visits) is the C10 with a detection rider.

questions.q: Which plan keeps paying if cancer goes into remission and comes back?
questions.means: The C10 is unit-based and continues to pay even if cancer returns.
questions.example: Like a season pass vs a single ticket. C10 is the season pass.
questions.why: Training: the C10 will continue to pay even if cancer comes back.
whyNot: The C20 ends after its one lump sum.
The A71000 is accident-only. It doesn't pay for cancer.

questions.q: The detection rider attaches to which plan?
questions.means: The C10 can have a detection rider. With it, it also covers treatments, up to 500 visits.
questions.example: Like an add-on that only fits one phone model.
questions.why: Training: the C10 can have a detection rider attached.
whyNot: The C20 has no detection rider structure.
The A71000 is an accident plan.

questions.q: C10 with a detection rider covers treatments like chemo and radiation up to how many visits?
questions.means: With a detection rider the C10 covers treatment visits, up to 500.
questions.example: 500 visits is years of treatment, which is why C10 is built for the long fight.
questions.why: Training: up to 500 visits for cobalt, radiation and chemotherapy.
whyNot: 50 is way too low.
365 is the A71000 hospital day limit.
questions.trick: Five hundred for the long fight.

questions.q: What license does Niko need to present and enroll a cancer plan?
questions.means: Cancer plans are health coverage, so a health producer license is required.
questions.example: Like needing a motorcycle license, not just a car license, to ride a bike.
questions.why: The 2.2 review flags 'agents don't need a Health license' as false.
whyNot: A life-only license covers life products, not cancer plans.
You always need a license to sell insurance.

questions.q: Best way to introduce the no-cost benefits?
questions.means: Always call them no-cost or pre-paid, never free. They were paid for through the member's group.
questions.example: 'Free' at a mall kiosk makes you walk faster. 'Already paid for' makes you stop.
questions.why: Training: 'These are no-cost benefits your group has provided for you.'
whyNot: 'Free' puts clients on guard and sounds worthless.
They come from the group, not from Niko personally.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · No-Cost Benefits We Provide

questions.q: The no-cost AD&D certificate pays how much?
questions.means: The AD&D certificate pays $2,000 to $4,000 depending on the member's group, for a covered accidental death or dismemberment.
questions.example: Enough for a used car down payment, not a funeral. That gap opens the real conversation.
questions.why: Training: pays $2,000 to $4,000, depending on the group.
whyNot: $10,000 to $50,000 is the B2000 base inside the paid A71000.
$25,000 is the Head Start floor.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · No-Cost Benefits We Provide

questions.q: What is AIL Plus?
questions.means: AIL Plus is a healthcare discount program, not insurance. One year at no cost, discounts at participating providers, 24/7 doctor consults.
questions.example: Like a store loyalty card: you still pay, just less.
questions.why: Training: a healthcare discount program, not insurance.
whyNot: It doesn't replace health coverage.
It's discounts, not a dental policy.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · No-Cost Benefits We Provide

questions.q: Which no-cost benefit lets parents name a guardian for their minor children?
questions.means: The Will Kit creates a basic will: who gets property, and a guardian for minor kids.
questions.example: Picking who drives your car if you can't.
questions.why: Training: lets parents name a guardian for their minor children.
whyNot: The Family Information Guide organizes accounts, debts and contacts.
The Child Safe Kit stores ID info in case a child goes missing.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · No-Cost Benefits We Provide

questions.q: Which no-cost benefit best reveals that the client's only coverage is through work?
questions.means: The Family Information Guide lists policies, accounts and debts, so you see coverage that could disappear with a job change.
questions.example: Like opening the glovebox and finding the insurance card has your boss's name on it.
questions.why: Training: the FIG shows what coverage they have and whether it's through work.
whyNot: The Will Kit reveals minor kids and planning, not current coverage.
The AD&D shows who depends on them through the beneficiary.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Maximizing the Value of No-Cost Benefits

questions.q: New Jersey free look on a new life policy (not a replacement)?
questions.means: The free look is the window to cancel a new policy for a full refund.
questions.example: Like a return window at a store.
questions.why: NJ: 10 days on a new policy.
whyNot: 30 days is the free look when the policy replaces an existing one.
3 days is a cooling-off period for other purchases, not NJ life.

questions.q: NJ free look when the new life policy REPLACES an existing one?
questions.means: Replacements get a longer free look so the client can be sure dropping the old policy is right.
questions.example: A bigger decision gets a longer return window.
questions.why: NJ: 30 days on a replacement.
whyNot: 10 days is for a normal new policy.
20 days isn't the NJ number.

questions.q: Life policy grace period after a missed premium?
questions.means: The grace period is how long the policy stays in force after a missed payment before it lapses.
questions.example: Like a phone bill that still works for a month after the due date.
questions.why: Standard life grace period: 31 days.
whyNot: 10 days is the NJ free look.
60 days is too long for a life policy grace period.
questions.trick: Grace = a month plus a day.

questions.q: How long can the company contest a life claim over a misstatement on the application?
questions.means: The contestability period is the window when the company can review the application after a death claim.
questions.example: Like a 2-year warranty, but for the application's honesty.
questions.why: Life policies: 2 years from issue.
whyNot: 1 year is too short.
5 years is too long.

questions.q: NJ continuing education for a life & health producer?
questions.means: NJ producers need continuing education every 2 years to keep the license.
questions.example: Like a gym membership that requires check-ins to stay active.
questions.why: NJ: 24 hours every 2 years, including 3 of ethics.
whyNot: 12 a year with 1 ethics shorts the ethics hours.
30 hours with no ethics isn't the NJ rule.

questions.q: Client's plan is $17 a week. What is that per month?
questions.means: Weekly to monthly: multiply by 52, divide by 12.
questions.example: A month isn't 4 weeks. It's about 4.33 weeks.
whyNot: $68 is $17 x 4. Months are longer than 4 weeks.
$70.83 is a math slip. Do 52 then divide by 12.

questions.q: Policy is $80 a month of life + $20 a month of A71000. What's the ALP?
questions.means: ALP is the monthly LIFE premium x 12. Per Niko's notes, the A71000 isn't counted.
questions.example: Your rent counts toward the lease, the parking spot doesn't.
questions.why: $80 x 12 = $960. The $20 A71000 is left out.
whyNot: $1,200 counts the A71000 too.
$480 is only 6 months.
questions.verify: Late Dec 2026 ALP becomes AP and A71 goes on every policy. Ask Nika how AP counts A71.

questions.q: On a 50% contract, a sale has $1,200 ALP. About what's the commission?
questions.means: Commission is roughly ALP x your contract percentage.
questions.example: Half the pie on a 50% contract.
questions.why: $1,200 x 50% = $600. It's an advance, so a lapse can mean a chargeback.
whyNot: $1,200 is the whole ALP, not your cut.
$300 would be a 25% contract.

questions.q: To turn a $65/month premium into a weekly number, you divide by what?
questions.means: There are about 4.33 weeks in a month (52 / 12).
questions.example: Rent split by weeks: $65 / 4.33 is about $15 a week.
whyNot: Dividing by 4 assumes 4-week months and overstates the weekly cost.
Dividing by 12 turns a yearly number into monthly.

questions.q: Does the child rider premium count toward ALP?
questions.means: Per Niko's notes, ALP includes the child rider, while the A71000 is excluded.
questions.example: The child rider rides on the life policy, so it counts as life.
questions.why: Notes: A71 excluded, child rider included.
whyNot: Some riders count. The child rider does.
No waiting period on counting it.

questions.q: Client, 28, wants to be done paying by retirement but covered for life. Best fit?
questions.means: LPU65 is whole life you pay off by 65, with coverage for life.
questions.example: Paying off the car before retirement and keeping it.
questions.why: Done paying at 65, covered for life. That's LPU65.
whyNot: Term to 65 ends the coverage at 65.
20-year term ends at 48 for him.

questions.q: A roofer says, 'If I fall, I'm out of work for weeks.' Which plan speaks to that?
questions.means: The A71000 pays the client cash when they get hurt: ER, hospital days, ICU, plus recovery support.
questions.example: Getting hurt on the job and still paying rent.
questions.why: Training: a worker with physical or high-risk work, the A71000 'Get Hurt, Get Paid' speaks to their risk.
whyNot: The C20 pays on a cancer diagnosis, not an injury.
GIO lets you buy more life insurance later.
questions.trick: Risky job = Get Hurt, Get Paid.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Maximizing the Value of No-Cost Benefits

questions.q: Client, 72, has some health issues and got turned down elsewhere. What's often the best fit?
questions.means: Graded Benefit Whole Life has more lenient underwriting, built for seniors who may not qualify for standard.
questions.example: Like a starter credit card when your credit has dings.
questions.why: Training: Graded Benefit is often the best option for seniors with health issues.
whyNot: LPU65 pays up at 65. She's already 72.
20-year term isn't built for a senior final-expense need.

questions.q: Young couple, new baby, a mortgage. Per training, what three things do you focus on?
questions.means: Training's example: income replacement, paying off the house, and starting the child early with Head Start.
questions.example: Protect the paycheck, the roof and the kid.
questions.why: Training example: young couple with a new baby and a mortgage.
whyNot: Funeral and graded benefit fit seniors, not new parents.
Those are fine add-ons, but not the core focus training names.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Maximizing the Value of No-Cost Benefits

questions.q: Client's mom fought cancer twice. She wants coverage that stays with her if it ever comes back. Best fit?
questions.means: The C10 keeps paying through recurrence. The C20 pays once and ends.
questions.example: She needs the season pass, not the single ticket.
questions.why: Training: the C10 continues to pay if cancer returns.
whyNot: The C20 ends after one payout.
The A71000 is accident-only.
questions.trick: Comes back? C10 comes back too.

questions.q: Peter's 20/60/20 rule: which group makes you the money?
questions.means: Per Peter: 20% never buy, 60% need to be sold, 20% are lay-downs. The 60% is the paycheck.
questions.example: Gym sign-ups: the middle group shows up only if the trainer texts them.
questions.why: Peter: the money is in the 60%, won by mastering objections.
whyNot: The lay-downs sell themselves, but they're only 20%.
The bottom 20% never buy, even if they say they want it.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Per Peter's team, about how many scheduled follow-ups actually close?
questions.means: Peter's team found less than 2% of scheduled follow-ups close, so he goes for the no instead of fake appointments.
questions.example: Like 'let's grab lunch sometime': it almost never happens.
questions.why: Peter: less than 2%. His point is a hang-up beats a fake appointment.
whyNot: 20% is the 20/60/20 number.
Half is way too optimistic.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Per Peter, about how many people you talk to should move from the intro into a presentation?
questions.means: Peter's intro scoreboard: about 1 in 3. If you're far below, the intro is the problem.
questions.example: Like a batting average around .333.
questions.why: Peter: about 1 out of 3 people should go from intro to presentation.
whyNot: 1 in 10 is the warning sign, not the target.
2 in 3 would be unusual.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Peter's tonality pyramid: what's the foundation at the bottom?
questions.means: Empathy is the base because it's an emotional product. Curiosity is next. Expert is the top.
questions.example: The foundation of a house goes in first.
questions.why: Peter: empathy is the bottom, then curiosity, then expert.
whyNot: Curiosity is the middle: the first 30-60 seconds and objections.
Expert is the top: credibility, medical questions and the pitch.
questions.trick: Every Child Eats: Empathy, Curiosity, Expert (bottom up).
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Which tone does Peter use for credibility, the medical questions and the pitch?
questions.means: The expert tone is stern and confident, no question in your voice, no 'um'.
questions.example: A mechanic who Googles how to change your oil loses you.
questions.why: Peter: expert tone in credibility, medical questions and the pitch.
whyNot: Curiosity is for the intro and objections.
Empathy is for discovery and hard news.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Peter's objection framework: Acknowledge, ____, Dive deeper, Suggest.
questions.means: Isolate means narrowing it down: 'Is it more the price, or you're not sure you need it?'
questions.example: A doctor asks 'where does it hurt?' before treating.
questions.why: Peter: acknowledge, isolate, dive deeper, suggest and end with a question.
whyNot: The pattern interrupt is Loop 2 for booking-call objections.
Re-closing comes after the suggestion.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: On a booking call, what's Peter's Loop 2 move?
questions.means: Loop 2: acknowledge, a pattern interrupt about something that doesn't matter, then your next question.
questions.example: 'Oh my gosh, are the kids going crazy?' breaks the script in their head.
questions.why: Peter: Loop 1 acknowledge and move on, Loop 2 pattern interrupt, Loop 3 pump fake.
whyNot: The pump fake is Loop 3.
Acknowledge and move on is Loop 1.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Spouse objection. After 'Which option would she tell you to go with?', what's the key question?
questions.means: 'Why do you think that?' makes him explain the reasons, so he sells himself.
questions.example: When a friend says 'my wife would want the bigger TV', asking why gets him to argue for it.
questions.why: Peter: the hypothetical, then 'And why do you think that?'
whyNot: Bringing her in can be fine, but it's not Peter's key question here.
That stalls the close instead of finishing it.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: 'I can't pay for it today.' What's Peter's key question?
questions.means: Ask what day they typically get paid, then line the first payment up with that day.
questions.example: Like setting rent autopay for the day after payday.
questions.why: Peter: 'What day do you typically get paid?'
whyNot: Someone else paying is its own objection with its own answer.
Hunting for another card pressures the client. Keep it clean.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Per Peter, at least how many times should you call every lead?
questions.means: Call every lead at least three times. People often pick up on the second or third dial.
questions.example: Like knocking: people answer on the second or third knock.
questions.why: Peter: dial every lead at least three times, double dial missed callbacks.
whyNot: One dial leaves most of the pickups on the table.
10 is more than Peter's minimum, and it can feel like harassment.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Per Peter's top producer playbook, what's constraint number one?
questions.means: 'You don't have an objection problem, you have an activity problem.' Track dials, presentations, sales and talk time.
questions.example: Like a basketball player who wants a better shot but only takes 20 shots a week.
questions.why: Peter: activity is constraint number one.
whyNot: Objections matter, but most agents who think that's the problem just haven't dialed enough.
Knowledge helps conviction, but activity comes first in his playbook.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: $100 A71000 level. Client cuts his hand, gets stitches at urgent care. Payout?
questions.means: ER and outpatient care pay half the level per injury, and urgent care for an injury counts as outpatient care.
questions.example: Half of a $100 bill is $50.
questions.why: Half of $100 is $50.
whyNot: $100 is the full level, which is one hospital day.
$0 would be right for sickness. A cut is an accident.

questions.q: $200 level. 14 days in the ICU, then discharged. Total ICU benefit?
questions.means: The first 14 ICU days pay double the level.
questions.example: Double $200 is $400 a day, times 14 days.
whyNot: $2,800 is $200 x 14, the normal hospital rate. ICU doubles it.
$8,400 is triple. Nothing in the A71000 pays triple.

questions.q: What's the difference between the no-cost AD&D certificate and the A71000?
questions.means: The AD&D certificate is a $2,000-$4,000 no-cost group benefit. The A71000 is a paid accident plan with hospital, ICU and ER cash plus the B2000.
questions.example: A free sample vs the product you buy.
questions.why: The certificate comes from the group at no cost. The A71000 has a premium.
whyNot: The certificate has no premium.
The A71000 is a paid plan with levels $100 to $500.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · No-Cost Benefits We Provide

questions.q: Training's nickname for the A71000?
questions.means: The A71000 is called the Get Hurt, Get Paid plan because it pays the client cash when an accident happens.
questions.example: Say it the way you'd say a slogan.
questions.why: Training: commonly known as the Get Hurt, Get Paid Plan.
whyNot: Freedom of Choice is a final-expense whole life plan.
Head Start is whole life on a child.

questions.q: A parent wants permanent coverage on their daughter that is HER OWN policy. Which fits?
questions.means: Head Start is the child's own whole life policy. The child rider is term coverage attached to the parent's policy.
questions.example: Her own phone line, not a line on your plan.
questions.why: Training: unlike the child rider, Head Start is the child's own permanent policy.
whyNot: The child rider is a rider on the parent's policy, not her own.
Spousal rider covers a spouse.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: The child rider is what kind of coverage?
questions.means: The child rider is term coverage: pure protection, no cash value.
questions.example: Renting, not owning.
questions.why: Training: considered a term coverage, pure protection with no cash value.
whyNot: Whole life on a child is Head Start.
It pays on death from any cause, not just accidents.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Children's Head Start + Deep Dive Children's Coverage

questions.q: Client asks: 'Does whole life ever expire if I keep paying?'
questions.means: Whole life is permanent coverage. As long as premiums are paid, it stays in force.
questions.example: Like owning the house: no lease ending.
questions.why: Training: permanent coverage that does not expire.
whyNot: Never quote an age that isn't on the policy. Say 'for life'.
65 is LPU65's last payment, not the end of coverage.
questions.trick: Whole life: say 'for life', never an age.

questions.q: Graded Benefit Whole Life, $10,000 face. Death 8 months after issue. Payout?
questions.means: Year 1 of a graded benefit policy pays 25% of the face.
questions.example: A quarter of the pizza in year one.
whyNot: $5,000 is 50%, the year 2 amount.
$10,000 is full face, after year 3.

questions.q: Freedom of Choice: what's the funeral-home assignment for?
questions.means: The benefit can be assigned so the funeral home gets paid directly, so the family isn't fronting the bill.
questions.example: Like autopay straight to the restaurant instead of handing cash to your cousin to deliver.
questions.why: Per Niko's notes, the assignment sends money to the funeral home of the family's choice.
whyNot: It doesn't choose the cemetery.
Assignment doesn't change the premium.
questions.trick: Freedom of Choice: choose who gets paid.
questions.verify: Confirm the starter and inflation amounts ($15k / $25-30k) with Nika.

questions.q: Shortest renewable and convertible term AIL training lists?
questions.means: Training lists a 4-year renewable and convertible term.
questions.example: A short lease with an easy re-up.
questions.why: Training: 4-Year Renewable and Convertible Term.
whyNot: No 1-year term is listed.
10-year is R&C too, but it isn't the shortest.

questions.q: Honest line when a client asks what happens to term when it ends?
questions.means: Term is temporary. When it ends, coverage ends. Say the honest version: most people outlive their term.
questions.example: Renters don't get the rent back when they move out.
questions.why: Per Niko's do-say list: 'most people outlive their term'.
whyNot: Term has no cash value, nothing comes back.
Conversion is a choice the client makes, not automatic.

questions.q: Can ADB be sold on its own at AIL?
questions.means: ADB can be sold on its own, but it's commonly an add-on to a base life policy.
questions.example: Fries can be ordered alone, but they usually come with the burger.
questions.why: Training: while ADB can be sold on its own, it is commonly an add-on.
whyNot: It isn't rider-only.
The A71000 has its own built-in B2000, a separate thing.
questions.trick: ADB: alone is allowed, add-on is normal.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Deep Dive Accidental Death Benefits

questions.q: Why is ADB sometimes called 'double indemnity'?
questions.means: The ADB can be set equal to the base face amount, so an accidental death pays double.
questions.example: A $50k base + $50k ADB = $100k if the death is accidental.
questions.why: Training: ADB can be added to equal the base face amount, so the beneficiary gets twice as much.
whyNot: It pays once, on death.
It covers the insured, not two people.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Deep Dive Accidental Death Benefits

questions.q: What does the Child Safe Kit app actually store?
questions.means: Parents record a photo, description, fingerprints and medical details, ready for police if a child goes missing.
questions.example: A ready-to-go file on your phone for the worst day.
questions.why: Training: a no-cost app for parents to record their child's identifying information.
whyNot: It isn't a policy.
It isn't money.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · No-Cost Benefits We Provide

questions.q: How long is the no-cost AIL Plus membership?
questions.means: AIL Plus comes as a one-year membership at no cost to the member.
questions.example: A one-year pass.
questions.why: Training: one-year membership provided at no cost.
whyNot: Not six months.
Not lifetime.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · No-Cost Benefits We Provide

questions.q: Where do the no-cost benefits sit in the presentation?
questions.means: They come early: they deliver value, build trust, produce referrals, and tell you what the family needs before you recommend anything.
questions.example: A doctor asks questions before writing the prescription.
questions.why: Training: rushing through the no-cost benefits to get to the sale loses trust, information and referrals.
whyNot: After the close is too late to learn what they need.
They're a planned step, not optional.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Maximizing the Value of No-Cost Benefits

questions.q: A 'trial app' at AIL means what?
questions.means: A trial app goes to underwriting without drafting money; drafting starts once approved. It's for uncertain health. The free look is a separate NJ rule.
questions.example: Test-driving before you sign the loan.
questions.why: Per Niko's notes: sent to underwriting without drafting, draft once approved.
whyNot: The free look is the 10-day cancel window after issue.
There's no 30-day test period.

questions.q: AIL's A.M. Best rating, said correctly?
questions.means: AIL is rated A (Excellent) by A.M. Best. Saying A+ overstates it.
questions.example: Say the grade on the report card, not a better one.
questions.why: Niko's do-say list: A (Excellent) A.M. Best, not A+.
whyNot: A+ is a different, higher rating AIL doesn't hold.
AAA is an S&P-style label, not A.M. Best's.
questions.src: Company facts in Niko's notes (AIL public pages)

questions.q: How much did AIL pay in life claims last year, per the credibility line?
questions.means: The honest credibility line: AIL paid over $287 million in life claims last year.
questions.example: Big number, say it fast and confident.
questions.why: Niko's notes: $287,140,775 in life claims in 2025.
whyNot: $95 billion is the coverage in force, not claims paid.
$28 million is ten times too small.
questions.src: Company facts in Niko's notes (AIL public pages)

questions.q: AIL was founded in what year, and unions since when?
questions.means: AIL started in 1951 and has worked with unions since 1961.
questions.example: Ten years in, the union label came on.
questions.why: Niko's company notes: founded 1951, unions since 1961.
whyNot: Off by ten years.
Off by ten years the other way.
questions.src: Company facts in Niko's notes (AIL public pages)

questions.q: $9.50 a week. Monthly?
questions.means: Weekly x 52 / 12.
questions.example: A month is 4.33 weeks, not 4.
whyNot: $38 is x4, which shortchanges the month.
$47.50 is x5, too many weeks.

questions.q: Niko wants about $10k in 3 months on a 50% contract. Roughly how many sales a week?
questions.means: At typical ALPs, 50% commission on 1-2 sales a week gets to about $10k over 3 months.
questions.example: Not a dial-a-thon, a steady one or two a week.
questions.why: Niko's own math: ~$10k in 3 months is about 1-2 sales a week.
whyNot: 5-6 a week would be far above the target.
10+ is a top-producer week, not the $10k math.
questions.trick: Ten grand = one or two a week.

questions.q: Hour Power: a $130/month plan is about how much a week?
questions.means: Monthly / 4.33 gives the weekly cost.
questions.example: $130 split over 4.33 weeks.
whyNot: $32.50 divides by 4.
$26 divides by 5.

questions.q: Client's only life coverage is through her job. What's the angle?
questions.a: It can vanish with the job
questions.means: Work coverage can disappear with a job change or layoff. Coverage she owns stays with her.
questions.example: A company phone goes back when you leave.
questions.why: Training: show how work coverage can disappear with a job change, and why coverage they own matters.
whyNot: Work coverage alone usually isn't enough and isn't hers.
Never advise replacing. Add owned coverage alongside.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Maximizing the Value of No-Cost Benefits

questions.q: Single parent, worried about the kids. Per training, what's the focus?
questions.means: Focus on guaranteed protection for the children's future, and naming a guardian through the Will Kit.
questions.example: Who raises them, and what pays for it.
questions.why: Training's example: guaranteed protection for the kids and a guardian via the Will Kit.
whyNot: Grandkid legacy is the grandparent conversation.
A71 helps, but it's not the core of a single parent's need.
questions.src: Week 0 training 2.1 · Maximizing the Value of No-Cost Benefits

questions.q: Peter's four angles of value: burial, leave money, cheaper plan, and ____?
questions.means: Yes to any of the four means the client has a reason to buy today.
questions.example: Some people with graded policies want full coverage now, not in two years.
questions.why: Peter: cover burial, leave money, cheaper plan, get out of a waiting period.
whyNot: Cash value isn't one of his four.
Kids aren't one of his four.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Peter's four facts about a current policy: company, coverage, monthly cost, and ____?
questions.means: Without all four you can't compare apples to apples.
questions.example: Like comparing phone plans: carrier, data, price, contract.
questions.why: Peter: who they're with, how much, what they pay, and whether there's a waiting period.
whyNot: The agent's name doesn't change the comparison.
Cash value isn't one of his four.
questions.trick: Who, how much, how much a month, waiting?
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: 'Kill the zombies' means what?
questions.means: Handle objections before the numbers: 'If I find something comfortable and affordable, would anything hold you back from seeing if you qualify today?'
questions.example: Lock the doors before the zombies show up.
questions.why: Peter: handling objections before they come up, before the price.
whyNot: It's not about hanging up.
Never skip medical questions.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Peter's pitch order?
questions.means: Package first, then the value in their words from discovery, then the price last.
questions.example: Show the car, talk about the road trips, then the payment.
questions.why: Peter: package, value, price, and 'if you can even get qualified'.
whyNot: Price first makes it a price conversation.
Value before the package has nothing to attach to.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: Peter's budget check line?
questions.means: 'I always want to make sure I'm not taking any food off the table. Is that comfortable every single month?'
questions.example: A caring check, not a push.
questions.why: Peter: 'not taking any food off the table'.
whyNot: 'Can you swing it' sounds like pressure.
'A dollar a day' is a line Niko's sheet cut: not everyone can.
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: 'I want to shop around.' Peter's first question after acknowledging?
questions.means: Ask what they're mainly looking for: lowest price, most coverage, or no waiting period. Then 'how will you know which company is right?'
questions.example: Find out what they're shopping FOR.
questions.why: Peter: 'What are you mainly looking for: lowest price, most coverage, or no waiting period?'
whyNot: Who else they're calling doesn't move the sale.
Budget is the next objection, not this one.
questions.trick: Shop around = what are you shopping for?
questions.src: Peter Roberts video (his style and stats, not AIL policy)

questions.q: 'I want to see it in writing.' Peter's first question?
questions.means: 'What specifically do you want to see in writing that'll help you decide?' then 'anything else?' to find a hidden objection.
questions.example: Narrow it to the one thing they really want to see.
questions.why: Peter: ask what specifically, then 'is there anything else?'
whyNot: Mailing it ends the call with nothing.
Challenging trust kills rapport.
